content:
Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI last month, accusing the company behind ChatGPT of stealing trade secrets related to hardware development. Nearly a month later, OpenAI has finally issued a detailed response to multiple allegations from Apple, in the form of a blog post.

First, a brief recap of the events:

  • July 10: Apple filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that former Apple employees systematically stole Apple's trade secrets to help OpenAI develop its hardware business in the future.
  • July 10: OpenAI issued a brief statement in response: "We have no interest in any other company's trade secrets. We will remain focused on developing innovative technologies that empower users around the world."
  • July 14: OpenAI updated its response, stating that it had not seen any evidence supporting Apple's allegations.

Then on August 4, OpenAI published a blog post that evening, finally providing a more detailed account of the incident. The full text can be read here.

The article is titled "Apple is getting this wrong" (蘋果搞錯了), credited to OpenAI.

OpenAI's latest response opens by characterising the lawsuit as "reckless, aggressive, and surprisingly targeted":

OpenAI then appears to suggest that it was not formally notified of the issues before the lawsuit was filed, including details that had been reported prior to today:

They went on to publicly disclose the contents of email correspondence, which can be viewed on the page.

Subsequently, the response finally acknowledged some of the data access issues raised by Apple:

If you have read Apple's initial filing, you would know that Tang Tan (鄧坦) is one of the focal points of the complaint. OpenAI's response tonight defended him:

The remainder of the response consists of just two more paragraphs, before turning into screenshots of emails and iMessage conversations. Here is the concluding statement:

We wish Apple had raised these issues with us before filing suit, as we would have been happy to explain everything to them. We have taken the allegations in the lawsuit seriously and have expressed our willingness to work with Apple to resolve the matter. However, they have instead attempted to rewrite the narrative, including making vague accusations against other former employees, and are likely to continue doing so. Apple's request for a preliminary injunction is based on misinformation and is entirely unnecessary, as we neither have nor want any of their trade secrets. What interests us far more is developing innovative products and technologies that can push the frontier forward.

That is the situation so far. This is not a legal response, but in the three and a half weeks since Apple initially filed suit, this is the most OpenAI has said (or shown).

As a reminder, you can read OpenAI's latest response here, and revisit Apple's original complaint here.
